How ball python morph odds work

Every pairing question comes down to the same small piece of arithmetic repeated for each gene. This page shows it for the four kinds of gene the planner handles, with examples it recomputes. It is arithmetic on probabilities, not a promise about any one clutch.

1. Recessive genes (Albino, Clown, Piebald)

A baby needs a copy from each parent to show the trait, and a baby with one copy is a hidden het. Two hets give a quarter visual, half het and a quarter normal. A visual by a het gives half visual and half het.

2. Incomplete dominant genes (Pastel, Enchi, Fire)

One copy shows the trait. Two copies make the Super form. Two pastels give a quarter Super Pastel, half Pastel and a quarter normal; a Super Pastel bred to a normal gives all pastels.

3. Dominant and lethal-when-doubled genes (Pinstripe, Spider)

A dominant looks the same with one or two copies. A lethal one, like spider, loses the double-copy eggs: a quarter of a spider-by-spider clutch does not hatch.

4. Put genes together

Multiply the odds gene by gene. Two pastel het albinos give nine different outcomes: a quarter are Pastel het Albino, one in eight each for het Albino, Pastel, Albino Pastel and Super Pastel het Albino, and one in sixteen each for Normal, Albino, Super Pastel and Albino Super Pastel. The planner does this for every male and female you own, then prices each outcome.

Common questions

How do you work out ball python morph odds?

Treat every gene as its own site. A recessive gene needs two copies to show, so two hets give 25% visual, 50% het and 25% normal. An incomplete dominant shows with one copy and makes a Super form with two, so two pastels give 25% Super Pastel, 50% Pastel and 25% normal. Multiply the odds of each gene together to get the odds of a combination.

What does it mean that spider is lethal when doubled?

A double copy of the spider gene is reported not to hatch, so a spider-by-spider pairing loses about a quarter of its eggs and the rest are half spider and a quarter normal. The planner takes those eggs out of the expected hatchlings.

Why not pair two genes from the same group?

Genes that sit at the same site on the chromosome, such as the Lesser, Butter and Mojave group, do not follow independent odds, so the simple multiplication gives wrong answers. The planner refuses those pairings rather than guess.

BALL PYTHON MORPH PAIRING PLANNER · RUNS IN YOUR BROWSER · NOTHING UPLOADED

Which pairing is worth making this season?

List your females and males with their morphs and hets, add what each morph sells for, and the planner works out the genetics odds for every possible pairing, the expected hatchlings, the revenue after fees and raising cost, and ranks the pairings by expected profit or by the chance of the morph you are after.

The starter animals, genes and prices are examples: replace every price with what you really sell for, and check each gene's inheritance with the breeder who produced it. New to the maths? Read how ball python morph odds work, with a worked example.

1. Your animals

Write visual morphs plainly (Pastel, Clown), a Super form as Super Pastel, a proven recessive carrier as het Albino, and an unproven one with its chance, 66% het Clown. Leave the part after the bar empty for a normal.

2. What each outcome sells for

3. The clutch

How it works

Odds: every gene is its own site and is inherited independently. For each gene the planner works out the chance an egg gets zero, one or two copies from the two parents (a possible het passes the gene on with half its het chance), names the result by the gene's type, and multiplies across genes. Outcomes with the same look and the same hidden hets are merged.

Money: expected hatchlings of each outcome are eggs times hatch rate times its chance; revenue is that times its price less selling fees; profit is revenue less the raising cost per hatchling and the overhead per clutch. The chance of at least one of an outcome in a clutch is one minus the chance every egg misses.

Not modelled: genes at the same site (Lesser, Butter and Mojave, or Cinnamon and Black Pastel), which are refused; linkage; sex; infertile eggs beyond the hatch rate you enter; the price premium for a proven het; unproven hets inside a baby's name; market swings; and breeder health or welfare. Gene types follow common breeder convention and may be wrong or out of date for your line. Unverified against real clutches: the odds are checked against an independent gamete-by-gamete count and every result is re-checked for probabilities that add to one.

Common questions

Which ball python pairing should I make this season?

List your females and males with their morphs and hidden hets, add what each outcome sells for, and the planner works out the odds for every possible pairing, the expected hatchlings, the revenue after fees and raising costs, and ranks the pairings by expected profit per clutch. It uses standard Mendelian odds for each gene.

How are the odds calculated?

Each gene is treated as its own independent site. A recessive gene shows with two copies and hides as a het with one, an incomplete dominant shows with one copy and makes a Super form with two, a dominant looks the same with one or two copies, and a lethal dominant such as the spider type loses the double-copy eggs. The odds for every gene are multiplied together across all the genes in the pairing.

What does 66% het mean?

A possible het is a baby from a het-by-visual or het-by-het pairing that has not been proven. The planner treats a 66% het as carrying the gene with two-in-three odds, so it passes the gene on to one third of eggs. Breeders also write 50% poss het for the baby of a visual and a normal. Enter the percentage you have.

Why does it refuse some pairings?

Some genes sit at the same site on the chromosome, such as the Lesser, Butter and Mojave group, and Cinnamon with Black Pastel. Their odds are not independent, so a pairing that mixes them is refused instead of giving a wrong answer. Pair those animals by checking the breeder who produced the line.

Can I add my own morphs?

Yes. The gene table is editable text: name, then R for recessive, I for incomplete dominant, D for dominant or L for dominant that is lethal when doubled, then optional aliases and an optional allelic group. Check each gene's inheritance with the breeder or project that produced it before you rely on it.

Are the prices real?

No. The prices in the starter list are made-up examples. Enter what you actually sell each morph for. Any outcome you did not price uses the default price, and the planner tells you how much of the clutch fell into unpriced morphs.

Is my collection uploaded or stored?

No. Everything runs in your browser, nothing is sent to a server, there are no accounts, and nothing is saved when you close the page. Download the ranking as a CSV to keep it.
